expectations.text: In the source list, peer-reviewed research comes before weaker kinds of source such as news articles or preprints (within each group, if the list is grouped).
expectations.evidence: Sections appear in this order: "### Peer-reviewed articles", then "### Preprint", then "### Research organization reports"

expectations.text: Any news article, preprint, or other source that isn't peer-reviewed research comes with a plain reason why it's included or what to watch for. If there are none, this passes.
expectations.evidence: The Pew report has only a findings summary ("54% have used chatbots for schoolwork..."). It gives no reason for including the source and no caution. RAND does have a caution: "It reports what students say, not tested learning."

expectations.text: The reply says which sources (or how many) meet the assignment's requirement of at least 3 peer-reviewed sources.
expectations.evidence: The reply never mentions a requirement of at least 3 peer-reviewed sources. "Bastani, Klar and Brasken are the only three I found" counts high-school experiments, not sources that meet the requirement.

expectations.text: The reply does not show the user a rubric, a credibility score or rating (for example "7/10" or "Tier 2"), or named levels such as "strong evidence," "usable with care," or "not evidence on its own" presented as a rating system.
expectations.evidence: No scores, tiers or rating levels appear. Sources are labeled only by type, for example "**Peer-reviewed article**" and "**Preprint, not yet peer reviewed.**"

expectations.text: Every link or DOI in the reply points to a page the transcript shows Claude opened (fetched) during this session.
expectations.evidence: The reply links to "https://www.govtech.com/education/nature-retracts-oft-cited-paper-on-positive-impact-of-chatgpt", but the tool log shows no fetch of that page.

expectations.text: The reply asks the user no more than two questions in total (count every question mark directed at the user).
expectations.evidence: Only one question mark is directed at the user: "Who chooses how the chatbot gets used: the student, or the tool's design?" The other question marks are inside article titles.
